name: Toscana IGT

sheet.place: Toscana IGT covers the whole region and leaves winemakers free to choose their grapes. Many Super Tuscans use it because their blends did not fit the old Chianti rules.

claims.claim: Toscana IGT (now IGP) is a regional designation. Its production zone is the whole of Tuscany, with about ⟦area|32,900 to 33,400 acres|13,300 to 13,500 hectares⟧ of vines in use.

Law 164 of 1992 introduced the IGT category in Italy. It sits between the strict DOC and DOCG and the plain vino da tavola. The Toscana IGT disciplinare was issued by ministerial decree on 9 October 1995 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 25 October 1995).
Blended Toscana IGT wines may use any proportions of the grape varieties approved for Tuscany. A wine that names one variety on the label must be at least 85% of that variety.
The designation is large. The Consorzio Vino Toscana says over 4,000 producers, an average of about 640,000 hl declared a year and about 27% of Tuscany's wine output.

Consorzio Vino Toscana is recognised by the Ministry (Masaf) as the protection body for all Toscana IGT producers. It was formed on 10 June 2019. Its earlier forms were the Ente Tutela Vini dei Colli della Toscana Centrale (founded 22 November 1984 by Piero Antinori, Vittorio Frescobaldi and Ambrogio Folonari) and from 27 July 1995 the Ente Tutela Vini di Toscana.
The 1967 Chianti DOC rules set Sangiovese at 50 to 75% and required 10 to 30% white grapes. This blocked Sangiovese-Cabernet blends and 100% Sangiovese from using the Chianti name.

Sassicaia (Tenuta San Guido, Bolgheri) was the first. Mario Incisa della Rocchetta planted Cabernet Sauvignon in 1944. The first commercial wine was the 1968 vintage, released in 1971. It was sold as vino da tavola because Bolgheri had no DOC for red wine at the time.

Early Super Tuscans such as Sassicaia and Tignanello were sold as vino da tavola, the bottom rung. Law 164 of 1992 created the IGT level, and Toscana IGT followed in 1995. Many moved to it. Sassicaia went straight to a DOC in 1994.

Super Tuscan is an unofficial term, not recognised in the Italian classification. It describes Tuscan reds, often with Cabernet or Merlot, made outside the old DOC rules. Some are IGT Toscana, some are DOC (such as Bolgheri) and Sassicaia has its own DOC.
Bolgheri DOC dates from 1983, for white and rosé. Bolgheri Rosso and the Sassicaia subzone came in 1994.
Chianti Classico DOCG covers the zone set by a 1932 decree. It grew from the 1716 Chianti but is much larger. Toscana IGT covers the whole region.

Chianti Classico DOCG needs 80 to 100% Sangiovese for annata and Riserva, plus red grapes suited to Tuscany for the rest. No white grapes are listed. A rule change raises Gran Selezione to 90 to 100% Sangiovese, phased in over several harvests, with the rest limited to listed native reds (Colorino, Canaiolo, Ciliegiolo, Mammolo, Pugnitello, Malvasia Nera, Foglia Tonda, Sanforte) up to 10%.
White grapes were allowed in Chianti Classico until 2006. The 2006 vintage was the first without them. 100% Sangiovese was allowed from 1996, when Chianti Classico became its own DOCG.

Chianti Classico vineyards must be on hills, no higher than ⟦elev|2,300 feet|700 m⟧, on soils mostly of sandstone, limy marl, clay shale, sand and gravel. Valley floors and heavy Pliocene clays are excluded. Toscana IGT has no such restriction shown in the sources read.

Chianti Classico rules: annata wine is sold from 1 October of the year after the harvest. Riserva needs at least 24 months of aging, Gran Selezione at least 30, both with at least 3 months in bottle, counted from 1 January after the harvest.
Chianti got its DOC in 1967, with Classico as its historic zone. Chianti Classico became a DOCG in 1984 and got its own rules in 1996. Gran Selezione was approved in 2013 and took effect in 2014.
